topic: Day 1 · Peptic Ulcer Bleeding — The Commonest Killer
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Gastroenterology & Emergency Endoscopy
speakerBio: A therapeutic endoscopist who runs the out-of-hours bleeding rota. He teaches the peptic ulcer as an artery in an acid crater — mechanical control plus pH control, never one without the other.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

03:20. A 71-year-old man on low-dose aspirin and recently started naproxen for back pain is wheeled into resus after three episodes of coffee-ground vomiting and then a gush of fresh red blood. BP 96/58, HR 118, cool peripheries, and a black tarry stool on the trolley. His last drink was whisky. This is the bread-and-butter emergency of the medical take — and the single commonest cause of a fatal upper GI bleed. Tonight we dissect the peptic ulcer: why it bleeds, how to read it down the scope, and how to stop it.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

A bleeding peptic ulcer is an artery in the floor of an acid crater — you win by clotting the vessel mechanically and by turning off the acid that keeps dissolving the clot.

2 · Mechanism — the WHY behind the WHY 🧪

Three forces converge to breach the mucosal defence and expose a vessel:

  • Acid + pepsin — the corrosive baseline. Pepsin is only active at low pH; it digests the mucosal matrix and any clot that forms.
  • Helicobacter pylori — chronic antral gastritis and duodenal metaplasia; the dominant cause of duodenal ulcers. It disrupts mucosal bicarbonate defence and drives acid hypersecretion.
  • NSAIDs / aspirin — systemic COX-1 inhibition strips protective mucosal prostaglandins; the dominant cause of gastric ulcers and the driver in this man. Add an SSRI or anticoagulant and the risk multiplies.

Once the ulcer erodes deep enough, it reaches an artery in its base. The classic and most feared is the posterior duodenal bulb ulcer eroding into the gastroduodenal artery (GDA) — a large-calibre vessel that produces torrential, often recurrent bleeding. A lesser-curve gastric ulcer can erode the left gastric artery.

🎯 The vicious cycle — draw it out

Vessel erodes → bleeds → the body tries to seal it with platelet plug and fibrin clot → but the crater sits in a bath of acid and pepsin at low pH → clot is a poor structure at pH < 6, platelet aggregation fails below pH 5.4 and pepsin actively lyses the fibrin → clot dissolves → rebleeds. This is the entire pharmacological rationale for high-dose PPI: raise intragastric pH above 6, and the clot is allowed to mature and hold. The PPI does not cauterise anything — it protects the clot the endoscopist builds.

3 · First moves before the scope 🚑

  • Resuscitate first, scope second. Two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, correct coagulopathy. Restrictive transfusion: target Hb 70 g/L (Villanueva NEJM 2013 — restrictive strategy improved survival in acute upper GI bleeding; 80 g/L if cardiovascular disease).
  • Risk-stratify. Glasgow–Blatchford score (GBS) for triage — GBS 0–1 may be safe for outpatient management; higher scores predict need for intervention. Full Rockall after endoscopy for mortality.
  • Endoscopy timing: within 24 hours of presentation for all admitted UGIB (ACG 2021). The very early (<6–12 h) scope does not improve outcomes and may worsen them — resuscitate properly first (Lau NEJM 2020).
  • Pre-endoscopy PPI is optional and does not reduce mortality/rebleeding; it may downstage lesions. Do not let it delay the scope.
  • Erythromycin 250 mg IV ~30–90 min pre-scope — a prokinetic that clears the stomach of clot and improves mucosal views.
⚠️ Danger — the terlipressin reflex

Do not reach for terlipressin or band ligation reflexively in a cirrhotic-looking patient with haematemesis — but equally, if you cannot exclude varices, the vasoactive/antibiotic variceal bundle is started empirically until the scope tells you the source. Peptic-ulcer and variceal management diverge sharply; the scope is the arbiter.

4 · The Forrest classification — reading the ulcer down the scope 🔬

Described by John Forrest in 1974, this stigmata-based classification is the language of every endoscopy report and the single best predictor of rebleeding without treatment. It tells you who needs endoscopic therapy and who can be sent to the ward on oral PPI.

ForrestStigmaRebleed risk (untreated)Endoscopic therapy?
IaActive spurting arterial haemorrhage~80–90%Yes — high-risk
IbActive oozing (non-spurting)~10–30%Yes — high-risk
IIaNon-bleeding visible vessel (pigmented protuberance)~40–50%Yes — high-risk
IIbAdherent clot resistant to washing~20–30%Consider — see clot debate
IIcFlat pigmented spot (haematin)~5–10%No — low-risk
IIIClean base~2–5%No — low-risk
💡 Memory hook — high-risk = I and IIa (and the sticky clot)

Spurt, ooze, vessel — Forrest Ia, Ib, IIa — are the high-risk stigmata that mandate endoscopic haemostasis. Spot and clean base — IIc, III — go to the ward on oral PPI and can often be fed and discharged early. The adherent clot (IIb) is the argument at the coffee machine.

5 · The adherent-clot debate (Forrest IIb) 🩸

An adherent clot may hide a visible vessel (IIa) or nothing (IIc). Two schools: (1) vigorous irrigation to dislodge, then treat whatever lies beneath; or (2) mechanical removal (cold snare/guillotine after adrenaline injection) to expose and treat the underlying stigma. ACG 2021 suggests that endoscopic therapy of the clot base may be considered but medical therapy alone (high-dose PPI) is a reasonable alternative because the incremental benefit is modest and the bleeding risk of dislodging is real. Decision individualised to endoscopist skill and patient risk.

6 · Endoscopic haemostasis — combination therapy 🎯

The cardinal rule of ulcer haemostasis:

Adrenaline alone is never enough. Injection of dilute adrenaline (1:10,000) tamponades and vasoconstricts — but the effect is temporary. It must be combined with a second, definitive modality.

Adrenaline works by volume tamponade and vasospasm; as it wears off the vessel re-opens and rebleeds. Meta-analyses (e.g. Marmo, Calvet) show dual therapy roughly halves rebleeding, surgery and mortality versus adrenaline monotherapy. So: inject to gain control and a dry field, then apply a permanent method.

ModalityHow it worksNotes
Adrenaline injection (1:10,000)Tamponade + vasoconstrictionFirst step to gain a dry field — always add a 2nd modality. Never definitive alone.
Thermal — bipolar/heater probeCoaptive coagulation — presses vessel walls together and sealsContact method; classic second modality.
Through-the-scope clipsMechanical closure of the vesselExcellent for a visible vessel; preferred where the vessel is accessible.
Over-the-scope clip (OTSC)Large-bite mechanical closureACG 2021: consider for rebleeding after prior therapy — superior to standard in refractory cases.
Hemospray / TC-325Mineral powder forms a mechanical barrier over the bleeding surfaceRescue/adjunct, especially diffuse or hard-to-reach oozing and malignant bleeding; temporary — pairs with definitive therapy or bridges to angio.
💡 Pearl — inject, then secure

Think "adrenaline buys the field, the clip/probe wins the war." A dry visible vessel treated with adrenaline plus a clip or thermal probe is the standard of care for Forrest Ia/Ib/IIa.

7 · After haemostasis — high-dose PPI 💊

Having built the clot mechanically, protect it pharmacologically by driving intragastric pH > 6.

  • High-risk ulcers (Forrest Ia–IIb) after successful endoscopic therapy: IV PPI. Classic regimen — 80 mg omeprazole/pantoprazole bolus, then 8 mg/h infusion for 72 hours (Lau NEJM 2000 — reduced rebleeding).
  • Intermittent high-dose IV PPI (e.g. 80 mg bolus then 40 mg BD–TDS) is non-inferior to continuous infusion (Sachar meta-analysis, JAMA Intern Med 2014) and is endorsed by ACG 2021 as an acceptable, often more practical, alternative.
  • Low-risk ulcers (IIc, III): oral PPI, early feeding, early discharge — no infusion needed.
  • After 72 h, step down to oral PPI; continue for the ulcer-healing course.
🎯 Contrast — continuous vs intermittent PPI

Continuous (80 mg + 8 mg/h ×72 h): the trial-validated regimen, tightest pH control. Intermittent (80 mg then 40 mg BD/TDS): non-inferior on rebleeding, frees the pump, cheaper. Either is defensible after endoscopic therapy of a high-risk ulcer; both massively outperform low-dose or oral PPI in that window.

8 · When haemostasis fails — re-scope, angio, or surgery ⚔️

  • Rebleeding after initially successful endoscopy: ACG 2021 recommends a repeat endoscopy with attempt at haemostasis (often OTSC) rather than going straight to surgery — most are controlled endoscopically.
  • Second failure, or exsanguinating bleed: transcatheter arterial embolisation (TAE) by interventional radiology is now generally preferred over surgery where available — lower morbidity, comparable outcomes. The GDA is a classic embolisation target.
  • Surgery (under-running the vessel ± definitive ulcer surgery) is the final backstop when endoscopy and IR fail or are unavailable, or the patient is in extremis.

9 · The second-look debate 🔁

Routine scheduled second-look endoscopy (re-scoping everyone at 24 h regardless of clinical course) is not recommended in the era of high-dose PPI (ACG 2021) — it does not improve outcomes for the average patient and consumes resources. Reserve repeat endoscopy for clinical evidence of rebleeding, or consider it selectively in the very highest-risk lesions where the initial haemostasis was suboptimal. Treat the patient, not the calendar.

10 · Aftercare — never forget the cause 🧫

  • Test for H. pylori and treat if positive — eradication dramatically cuts recurrence. Note: acute bleeding lowers the sensitivity of biopsy urease tests, so a negative test in the bleeding setting must be repeated after recovery before H. pylori is excluded.
  • Review NSAIDs/aspirin. Stop the offending NSAID. If aspirin is for secondary cardiovascular prevention, restart it early (within ~3–5 days once haemostasis is secure) with PPI cover — stopping it outright raises cardiovascular death (Sung, Ann Intern Med 2010).
  • Repeat endoscopy at 6–8 weeks for gastric ulcers to confirm healing and exclude malignancy (biopsy the rim).
☠️ M&M — "The adrenaline held... for an hour"

A 68-year-old woman with a posterior duodenal ulcer, Forrest Ia spurting, was scoped by a tired on-call trainee at 02:00. He injected adrenaline, the field went dry, the spurt stopped, and — satisfied — he withdrew without applying a clip or thermal probe. She was started on an oral PPI on the ward. Ninety minutes later she vomited 800 mL of fresh blood, arrested, and was resuscitated to a second emergency scope that found the GDA bleeding freely; she went to IR for embolisation and survived with an ICU stay. Two errors: (1) adrenaline monotherapy on a high-risk vessel — it always needed a second modality (clip/thermal); and (2) an oral, not high-dose IV, PPI after a Forrest Ia lesion, so the fragile clot was never pH-protected. Lesson: for Forrest Ia–IIa, the two non-negotiables are combination endoscopic haemostasis and high-dose PPI. Adrenaline that "looks dry" is a trap — the vessel re-opens when it wears off.

11 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Mechanism: acid/pepsin + H. pylori + NSAIDs erode into an artery (classically posterior duodenal → GDA); acid lyses the clot → PPI raises pH > 6 to protect it.
  • Resuscitate first, scope within 24 h; transfuse to Hb 70 (80 if cardiac); erythromycin to clear the stomach.
  • Forrest: Ia spurt, Ib ooze, IIa visible vessel = high-risk, treat; IIc spot, III clean base = low-risk, oral PPI; IIb clot = debate.
  • Combination haemostasis: adrenaline to gain the field + a second modality (clip / thermal / hemospray). Adrenaline alone is never enough.
  • High-dose PPI after: 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/h ×72 h, or intermittent high-dose (non-inferior).
  • Rebleed → re-scope (± OTSC); failure → angio-embolisation; last resort surgery. No routine second-look.
  • Cure the cause: eradicate H. pylori (re-test after recovery), stop NSAIDs, restart secondary-prevention aspirin early under PPI cover, re-scope gastric ulcers to exclude cancer.

Next session: we cross into the harder territory of the cirrhotic — where the bleed is variceal, the physiology is portal, and transfusion itself can kill.

moderatorQs.q: Why is adrenaline injection alone considered inadequate for a Forrest Ia ulcer, and what must accompany it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because dilute adrenaline (1:10,000) achieves haemostasis only by volume tamponade and transient vasoconstriction — as the drug is absorbed and its effect wanes, the vessel re-opens and the ulcer rebleeds. Meta-analyses consistently show adrenaline monotherapy has a substantially higher rebleeding rate than combination therapy, which roughly halves rebleeding, surgery and mortality. It must therefore be paired with a second, definitive modality: a through-the-scope clip (mechanical closure), a thermal contact device (bipolar/heater probe coaptive coagulation), or hemospray as an adjunct. The mental model is 'adrenaline buys the dry field; the clip or probe delivers durable closure.' A high-risk vessel treated with adrenaline alone that 'looks dry' is a classic trap.

moderatorQs.q: Explain the physiological rationale for high-dose PPI after endoscopic haemostasis of a bleeding ulcer.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The bleeding vessel sits in a crater bathed in gastric acid and pepsin. Platelet aggregation is impaired below pH ~5.4 and the fibrin clot is unstable and actively lysed by pepsin, which is only proteolytically active at low pH. So even after the endoscopist has mechanically built a clot, an acidic environment dissolves it — the mechanism of early rebleeding. High-dose PPI (e.g. 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h infusion for 72 h, or intermittent high-dose which is non-inferior) raises intragastric pH above 6, allowing the platelet plug and fibrin to mature and hold. The PPI is not haemostatic itself — it is clot protection, which is why it is only high-value after successful endoscopic therapy of a high-risk (Forrest Ia–IIb) lesion.

moderatorQs.q: A patient rebleeds 18 hours after successful clipping of a duodenal ulcer. Walk us through the escalation pathway.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Resuscitate and correct coagulopathy first. The recommended next step (ACG 2021) is repeat endoscopy with a further attempt at haemostasis — not immediate surgery — because most rebleeds are controlled endoscopically; an over-the-scope clip (OTSC) is often superior to standard therapy in the re-treatment setting. If endoscopy fails again or the patient is exsanguinating, proceed to transcatheter arterial embolisation (TAE) by interventional radiology — the gastroduodenal artery is the classic target for a posterior duodenal ulcer — which is now generally preferred over surgery where available. Surgery (under-running the vessel) is the final backstop when endoscopy and IR fail or are unavailable. Routine scheduled second-look endoscopy is not recommended; you re-scope for clinical rebleeding, which this patient has.

audienceQs.q: How quickly should a stable patient with melaena and a suspected ulcer be scoped — is it a middle-of-the-night job?
audienceQs.answerHTML: For almost all admitted upper GI bleeds the target is endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation, after adequate resuscitation — not necessarily overnight. The evidence (Lau, NEJM 2020) showed that very early endoscopy (<6 h) does not improve outcomes and can worsen them if the patient is under-resuscitated. So the priority is haemodynamic stabilisation, correcting coagulopathy, transfusing to a restrictive Hb target of 70 g/L (80 if cardiovascular disease), and giving IV erythromycin ~30–90 min beforehand to clear the stomach. A truly exsanguinating, unstable bleed is the exception that warrants immediate scoping — but the stable melaena patient is best served by a properly prepared daytime/next-available list within that 24-hour window.

audienceQs.q: Should we really restart this patient's aspirin so soon after a bleeding ulcer?
audienceQs.answerHTML: If the aspirin is for secondary cardiovascular prevention (previous MI, stroke, stent), yes — restart it early, typically within about 3–5 days once haemostasis is secure, under PPI cover. The trial evidence (Sung, Ann Intern Med 2010) showed that patients whose aspirin was stopped after a bleeding ulcer had a small increase in rebleeding but a significantly higher all-cause and cardiovascular mortality — the thrombotic risk of withdrawal outweighed the bleeding risk of continuation. The offending NSAID (e.g. naproxen) should be stopped outright. If the aspirin were purely for primary prevention, the calculus differs and it can often be discontinued permanently.

audienceQs.q: The H. pylori biopsy urease test came back negative during the acute bleed — can we call the patient H. pylori-negative?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No. Acute upper GI bleeding significantly lowers the sensitivity of biopsy-based tests (rapid urease/CLO test and histology) — blood, the alkaline environment and recent PPI all suppress the organism and cause false negatives. A negative test in the bleeding setting must be repeated after recovery before H. pylori can be excluded, using a urea breath test or stool antigen (off PPI for ~2 weeks) or repeat biopsy. Because eradication dramatically reduces ulcer recurrence and rebleeding, missing a true-positive here is a real harm. Practically: if the acute test is positive, treat; if negative, arrange confirmatory testing at follow-up rather than declaring the patient negative.
